trap.wrong: "Sample 1% of traces at the start of each request."
trap.why: Random head sampling throws away most of the rare failed and slow traces you actually need.
trap.probe: Context propagation everywhere, including queues, tail-based sampling, attribute discipline, budgets.
trap.say: "W3C context through every hop including message headers, and tail sampling that keeps all errors and slow traces plus a small baseline, with per-team budgets."

thesis: Propagate trace context everywhere with a standard (W3C Trace Context via OpenTelemetry), keep the traces that matter with tail-based sampling (errors and slow requests at 100%, a small sample of normal ones), make span attributes queryable, and give teams a budget. You want every interesting trace, not every trace.
pitch: First, propagation: every service, queue and async hop must carry trace context, or traces break into fragments. I'd standardise on OpenTelemetry SDKs and W3C traceparent headers, including in message headers for Kafka or SQS. Second, sampling: head-based sampling decides at the start and is cheap, but randomly drops the rare slow or failed requests you most need. Tail-based sampling buffers spans in collectors and decides after the trace completes: keep all errors, all traces above a latency threshold, and maybe 1% of the rest. That keeps costs proportional to interesting traffic. Third, useful spans: consistent naming, attributes like tenant, endpoint and result that you can filter on, and links from metrics exemplars and logs to traces. Fourth, cost governance: per-team volume budgets, limits on attribute cardinality and span counts, and dropping noisy internal spans.

points.d: W3C Trace Context headers over HTTP and gRPC, and in message metadata for queues. A single service that drops context breaks every trace through it.
OpenTelemetry SDKs and auto-instrumentation for frameworks, clients and databases, with shared conventions for span names and attributes.
Decides at trace start with a fixed probability. Simple, low overhead, but misses rare failures unless rates are high.
Collectors buffer spans and decide per trace: keep errors, slow traces and a baseline sample. Needs collector capacity and trace-aware routing.
Endpoint, tenant tier, region, version and outcome as span attributes so you can ask 'slow traces for tenant X after deploy Y'.
Metric exemplars point to example traces; logs include trace ids; dashboards link to trace search.
Per-team span volume budgets, caps on spans per trace, and removing high-volume low-value spans (health checks, tight loops).

decision: OpenTelemetry with W3C context everywhere; tail-based sampling at the collector for production; head sampling only as a pre-filter at very high volumes. Measure trace completeness as a health metric.
numbers: Volume example: 20,000 req/s × 30 spans per trace = 600,000 spans/s. Keeping 100% of errors (say 0.5%), slow traces (1%) and 1% of the rest keeps about 2.5% of traces, roughly 15,000 spans/s.
Tail sampling buffer: collectors hold spans for the decision window (for example 10–30 seconds), which sizes their memory.
pitfalls: Async hops (queues, thread pools) that lose context.
Head sampling at 1% and wondering why no failed traces are captured.
High-cardinality attributes (user ids in span names) exploding storage and indexing.
Each team choosing different span names and attributes, making cross-service queries useless.

followups.q: How does tail sampling work with spans arriving at different collectors?
followups.a: Route all spans of a trace to the same collector instance (load-balance by trace id), then decide when the trace completes or times out.

followups.q: How do you trace through Kafka?
followups.a: Put trace context in message headers; the consumer starts a span linked to the producer's span, since processing may happen much later.

followups.q: What's a good baseline sampling rate?
followups.a: Enough to see normal behaviour per endpoint: often 1–5% of successful traces, adjusted per service by volume.

example: A payments platform with 60 services moved from 0.1% head sampling to tail sampling that keeps all errors and all traces above 1 second plus 2% of the rest. Tracing cost fell 40% while engineers could now find a trace for nearly every customer-reported failure.
